doc.title: Cal Collins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 11, 1997

title: Recent recordings and running his own quartet
summary: He discusses Ohio Style, Tenderly, a Wes Montgomery tribute and a Bob Barnard session, and the cost of self-contained groups.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Well your most recent — is it “Ohio Style” — is that your most recent record?

As a leader it is. The other, a couple more as a co-leader, let’s see I’m on a thing called “Tenderly,” what label do they call that? I think it’s an independent type owned thing. And oh I did that tribute to Wes Montgomery thing with a whole bunch of us, a whole bunch of guitar players did a tribute to Wes Montgomery. That was released in Tokyo long before it was released over here — about a year or so, before it was released over here. That was really the last thing major that I did and this other one, “Tenderly,” and then I’ve got a thing coming up — how is that?

Oh yeah, that’s the other — yeah. There’s an Australian trumpet player, Bob Barnard? And I did a recording with him, less than two years ago in New York. I think that was on a Canadian label, oh I forgot the name of it, Sackville or something like that?
Sackville it was, yeah. It was on Sackville.
Well with the “Ohio” album, you used your own group? It sounded great too.

Yeah that was a real nice one. I used the quartet that I’ve used around the Cincinnati area, and once in a while we do go out as a self-contained group but not too often. When you get into a self-contained group, you’re talking about money, headaches, this and that you know.
Yeah. It’s hard to keep a band working enough that you can tell all the fellows, stick with me.
How many is there? Phil Woods. Oscar Peterson’s trio. Dave Brubeck. That’s about it, you know, self-contained groups.
